ohm-and-bit.title: Ampwright Labs demonstrates solid-state battery cells for phones
ohm-and-bit.author: Rafe Okonkwo-Hart
body: [f01: Ampwright Labs showed off solid-state battery cells built for phones on Thursday.] [f03: Instead of a liquid electrolyte, the cells use a thin ceramic layer to carry ions between the electrodes.]
[f02: Ampwright says the cells store 1,050 Wh per liter.] That's the number phone makers care about, because it decides how much battery fits behind a screen.
[f04: The company also claims the cells charge to 80% in 12 minutes.] [f05: In Ampwright's own tests, a cell kept 90% of its capacity after 1,200 charge cycles.]
Now the limits. Ceramic is hard to make thin and even, and one crack can ruin a cell. Building a few demo cells is one thing; building millions of them is the hard part.

byteward.title: Ampwright Labs shows off solid-state battery cells for phones
byteward.author: Dana Whitlock
body: [f01: Ampwright Labs on Thursday showed solid-state battery cells designed for smartphones.] [f02: The company says they store 1,050 Wh per liter.]
[f06: Ampwright plans to begin mass production in 2028.] That means the first phones with these cells are still a long way off.
Solid-state batteries have been promised for years, so the proof will be in shipping products.

launch-desk.title: Ampwright Labs shows solid-state battery cells for phones
launch-desk.author: Inez Calder
body: [f01: Ampwright Labs has shown solid-state battery cells for phones.] [f07: The startup also announced $310 million in new funding.] [f08: The round values it at $2.1 billion.]
[f09: Ampwright will open a pilot production line in 2027.] [f06: Mass production is planned for 2028.]
That's an aggressive timeline for a technology known for slipping, and investors will be watching the pilot line closely.
